body:
in Chemistry |   	August 31st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
The Peri­od­ic Table of Ele­ments lists the 118 chem­i­cal ele­ments that make up every­thing in our world. Some you’re famil­iar with—Hydrogen, Oxy­gen, Nitro­gen, etc. Oth­ers maybe less so—Vanadium, Ger­ma­ni­um, and Yttri­um.
Accord­ing to the Amer­i­can Chem­i­cal Soci­ety, 44 of those 118 ele­ments might dis­ap­pear by cen­tu­ry’s end. Enter the Peri­od­ic Table of Endan­gered Ele­ments (shown above). The most endan­gered ones, high­light­ed in red, are Zinc, Gal­li­um, Ger­ma­ni­um, Arsenic (is this a good or very bad thing?), Sil­ver, Indi­um, Tel­luri­um, and Hafni­um. Made avail­able under a Cre­ative Com­mons license, the Peri­od­ic Table of Endan­gered Ele­ments can be viewed in a larg­er for­mat here.

The orig­i­nal image (top of the page), cre­at­ed in 2015, was updat­ed by EuChemS in 2023 (above). The updat­ed table fea­tures the cur­rent-day avail­abil­i­ty of all 90 ele­ments, rather than just the endan­gered 44 ele­ments, adds an axis for sus­tain­abil­i­ty, and flags ele­ments used in smart­phone pro­duc­tion.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: Tim Curry (RIP) Breaks Down His Most Iconic Roles: Rocky Horror, Clue, Muppet Treasure Island & More
description:
in Film, Television |   	August 31st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Upon hear­ing of Tim Cur­ry’s death last week, some of us could recall hav­ing
body:
in Film, Television |   	August 31st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Upon hear­ing of Tim Cur­ry’s death last week, some of us could recall hav­ing seen him on stage: in Amadeus or Spa­malot on Broad­way, per­haps, though he also drew acclaim in the work of Stop­pard, Brecht, and Shake­speare. For many more of us — per­haps all of us — it was his most mem­o­rable film and tele­vi­sion per­for­mances that sprang to mind. To an extent, which ones are most mem­o­rable depends on the view­er. Some will for­ev­er remem­ber Cur­ry as DJ John­ny LaGuardia in Times Square, the deceit­ful Roman­ian phil­an­thropist in Con­go, the arch-neme­sis King Chick­en on Duck­man, or even as the Bard him­self in the series Will Shake­speare.
More will remem­ber him as Dr. Frank-N-Furter, the cross-dress­ing mad sci­en­tist from the plan­et Trans­sex­u­al at the cen­ter of the stage musi­cal The Rocky Hor­ror Show as well as its film adap­ta­tion The Rocky Hor­ror Pic­ture Show. The lat­ter end­ed up becom­ing the much larg­er-scale cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non, still screened at mid­night to this day, more than half a cen­tu­ry after its the­atri­cal release.
In that time, the audi­ence-par­tic­i­pa­tion rit­u­als have grown elab­o­rate enough to over­shad­ow the con­tent. Still, if you real­ly try to focus on the action onscreen, you’ll notice the remark­able extent to which — even now that all the tropes of sci­ence-fic­tion B movies, nine­teen-fifties teen cul­ture, and delib­er­ate glam-rock excess have become bare­ly rec­og­niz­able — Cur­ry’s per­for­mance remains vital.
Just six months ago, the Acad­e­my of Motion Pic­ture Arts and Sci­ences put up a video in which Cur­ry looks back at his defin­ing roles. The list begins, nat­u­ral­ly, with Rocky Hor­ror, but also includes his turns as the Lord of Dark­ness in Leg­end (which he was offered after Rid­ley Scott saw him as Dr. Frank-N-Furter), Pen­ny­wise in Stephen King’s It (now regard­ed as the ne plus ultra of evil clown char­ac­ters), and Long John Sil­ver in Mup­pet Trea­sure Island (his per­son­al favorite of his movies). We’re also told of parts he did­n’t get, like Ian Mal­colm in Juras­sic Park, for which he was con­sid­ered, or — more tan­ta­liz­ing­ly — Han­ni­bal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, whom he “des­per­ate­ly want­ed to play.” He also offhand­ed­ly men­tions that, in addi­tion to Clue’s three exist­ing end­ings, he also shot a fourth in which his but­ler is revealed to have com­mit­ted all the mur­ders. “Of course, that was my favorite,” he says. Alas, “they nev­er released that end­ing, because they thought it was too obvi­ous.”
via Laugh­ing Squid

title: Milton Glaser’s 10 Rules for Life & Work: The Celebrated Designer Dispenses Wisdom Gained Over His Long Life & Career
description:
in Creativity, Design, Life |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in Creativity, Design, Life |   	September 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	
	

“None of us has real­ly the abil­i­ty to under­stand our path until it’s over,” the cel­e­brat­ed graph­ic design­er Mil­ton Glaser mused less than a minute into the above video.
The late Mil­ton Glaser’s many con­tri­bu­tions to pop culture—the I ❤ NY logo, the psy­che­del­ic por­trait of a rain­bow-haired Bob Dylan, DC Comics’ clas­sic bul­let logo—con­ferred unde­ni­able author­i­ty. To the out­side eye, he seemed to have a pret­ty firm han­dle on the path he trav­eled for lo those many decades. Aspi­rant design­ers would do well to give extra con­sid­er­a­tion to any advice he might have shared.
As would the rest of us.
His “Ten Things I Have Learned,” orig­i­nal­ly deliv­ered as part of a talk to the AIGA—a ven­er­a­ble mem­ber­ship orga­ni­za­tion for design professionals—qualifies as sol­id life advice of gen­er­al inter­est.
Yes, the Inter­net spawns bul­let-point­ed tips for bet­ter liv­ing the way spring rains yield mush­rooms, but Glaser, a self-described “child of mod­ernism,” did not truck in pithy Insta­gram-friend­ly apho­risms. Instead, his list was born of reflec­tion on the var­i­ous turns of a long and most­ly sat­is­fy­ing cre­ative career.
We’ve excerpt­ed some of his most essen­tial points below, and sug­gest that those read­ers who are still in train­ing give spe­cial empha­sis to num­ber sev­en. Don’t place too much weight on num­ber nine until you’ve estab­lished a sol­id work eth­ic. (See num­ber four for more on that.)
MILTON GLASER”S TEN RULES FOR WORK AND LIFE (& A BONUS JOKE ABOUT A RABBIT).
1. YOU CAN ONLY WORK FOR PEOPLE THAT YOU LIKE
Some years ago I real­ized that… all the work I had done that was mean­ing­ful and sig­nif­i­cant came out of an affec­tion­ate rela­tion­ship with a client.
2. IF YOU HAVE A CHOICE NEVER HAVE A JOB
Here, Glaser quotes com­pos­er John Cage: Nev­er have a job, because if you have a job some­day some­one will take it away from you and then you will be unpre­pared for your old age. 
3. SOME PEOPLE ARE TOXIC AVOID THEM.
Glaser rec­om­mends putting a ques­tion­able com­pan­ion to a gestalt ther­a­py test. If, after spend­ing time with that per­son “you are more tired, then you have been poi­soned. If you have more ener­gy, you have been nour­ished. The test is almost infal­li­ble and I sug­gest that you use it for the rest of your life.”
4. PROFESSIONALISM IS NOT ENOUGH (or THE GOOD IS THE ENEMY OF THE GREAT)
Glaser con­cedes that a record of depend­able excel­lence is some­thing to look for in a brain sur­geon or auto mechan­ic, but for those in the arts, “con­tin­u­ous trans­gres­sion” is the qual­i­ty to cul­ti­vate. Pro­fes­sion­al­ism does not allow for that because trans­gres­sion has to encom­pass the pos­si­bil­i­ty of fail­ure and if you are pro­fes­sion­al your instinct is not to fail, it is to repeat suc­cess. 
5. LESS IS NOT NECESSARILY MORE
I have an alter­na­tive to the propo­si­tion that I believe is more appro­pri­ate. ‘Just enough is more.’
6. STYLE IS NOT TO BE TRUSTED
Style change is usu­al­ly linked to eco­nom­ic fac­tors, as all of you know who have read Marx. Also fatigue occurs when peo­ple see too much of the same thing too often.
7. HOW YOU LIVE CHANGES YOUR BRAIN
The brain is the most respon­sive organ of the body…. Thought changes our life and our behav­ior. I also believe that draw­ing works in the same way…. Draw­ing also makes you atten­tive. It makes you pay atten­tion to what you are look­ing at, which is not so easy.
8. DOUBT IS BETTER THAN CERTAINTY
One of the signs of a dam­aged ego is absolute cer­tain­ty. Schools encour­age the idea of not com­pro­mis­ing and defend­ing your work at all costs. Well, the issue at work is usu­al­ly all about the nature of com­pro­mise…. Ide­al­ly, mak­ing every­one win through acts of accom­mo­da­tion is desir­able.
9. IT DOESN’T MATTER
Glaser cred­its essay­ist Roger Rosenblatt’s Rules for Aging (misiden­ti­fy­ing the title as Aging Grace­ful­ly) with help­ing him artic­u­late his phi­los­o­phy here.  It doesn’t mat­ter what you think. It does not mat­ter if you are late or ear­ly, if you are here or there, if you said it or didn’t say it, if you are clever or if you were stu­pid. If you were hav­ing a bad hair day or a no hair day or if your boss looks at you cock­eyed or your boyfriend or girl­friend looks at you cock­eyed, if you are cock­eyed. If you don’t get that pro­mo­tion or prize or house or if you do – it doesn’t mat­ter.
10. TELL THE TRUTH
It’s inter­est­ing to observe that in the new AIGA’s code of ethics there is a sig­nif­i­cant amount of use­ful infor­ma­tion about appro­pri­ate behav­ior towards clients and oth­er design­ers, but not a word about a designer’s rela­tion­ship to the pub­lic. If we were licensed, telling the truth might become more cen­tral to what we do.
BONUS JOKE
A butch­er was open­ing his mar­ket one morn­ing and as he did a rab­bit popped his head through the door. The butch­er was sur­prised when the rab­bit inquired ‘Got any cab­bage?’ The butch­er said ‘This is a meat mar­ket – we sell meat, not veg­eta­bles.’ The rab­bit hopped off. The next day the butch­er is open­ing the shop and sure enough the rab­bit pops his head round and says ‘You got any cab­bage?’ The butch­er now irri­tat­ed says ‘Lis­ten you lit­tle rodent, I told you yes­ter­day we sell meat, we do not sell veg­eta­bles and the next time you come here I am going to grab you by the throat and nail those flop­py ears to the floor.’ The rab­bit dis­ap­peared hasti­ly and noth­ing hap­pened for a week. Then one morn­ing the rab­bit popped his head around the cor­ner and said ‘Got any nails?’ The butch­er said ‘No.’ The rab­bit said ‘Ok. Got any cab­bage?’’
Read Mil­ton Glaser’s “Ten Things I Have Learned” in its entire­ty here.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.
Relat­ed Con­tent:
Mil­ton Glaser Draws Shake­speare & Explains Why Draw­ing is the Key to Under­stand­ing Life

title: Marka27 Superimposes Pop Culture, Graffiti, and Political Critique in Urgent Portraits
description: Animated characters, patterned textiles, logos from iconic fashion labels, graffiti, and more coalesce in the vibrant portraits of Victor Quiñonez
body:
Animated characters, patterned textiles, logos from iconic fashion labels, graffiti, and more coalesce in the vibrant portraits of Victor Quiñonez. Born in Mexico, raised in East Dallas, and now based in Brooklyn, the artist, who works as Marka27, is interested in the ways activism and pop culture converge, and he infuses the visual language of contemporary street art with Indigenous imagery and Mexican mural traditions. Whether working on large-scale walls or more intimate canvases, Quiñonez taps into his own experiences of living between cultures and the arbitrary nature of national borders.
Portraits like “Luchando Por Mi Alma” superimpose the signature Louis Vuitton pattern, desert flora, a striped weaving, a masked Lucha Libre figure, and a stereotypical, low-wage character from the television show Family Guy atop a portrait of a man in a wide-brimmed hat. This pastiche is emblematic of what Quiñonez dubs his “neo Indigenous” style in which potent cultural symbols and a critical consideration of the social and political landscape converge.
Installation view of ‘Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá’ in Boston (2025)
In his solo exhibition Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá, which translates to “not from here, not from there,” the artist presents several portraits alongside a collection of sculptures and immersive installations. Following its debut at Boston University in 2025, the exhibition traveled to the University of North Texas in Denton, where it was on view briefly before being shut down by the administration. Now at its third venue, Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá will open at Institute of the Arts and Sciences in Santa Cruz this October. 
The censored show is explicitly critical of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with the artist’s I.C.E. Scream series confronting the mandate. This particular body of work includes a street vendor’s pushcart and sculptural paletas, one of which encases handcuffs in its translucent resin body with a faint image of a person in a cage imprinted on the oversized stick. Smaller acrylic iterations contain photographic portraits of street vendors embedded within. Etched onto the wooden sticks are a government logo paired with a mock agency called “U.S. Inhumane and Cruelty Enforcement.” By placing portraiture at the center of every work large and small, the artist directs our attentions to the very people most impacted by these actions, while emphasizing our shared humanity.
“At first glance, you’re like, ‘Oh, wow, that’s a popsicle.’ You want to approach it. It brings back nostalgia for everyone. It symbolizes something fun, innocent and childlike,” Quiñonez told The Los Angeles Times. “But then when you get closer, you see the writing on the popsicle sticks. … I wanted to show the two different sides of the world that we’re living in.”
In addition to his studio works, the artist has painted murals in cities across the U.S., which you can explore more of on his website and Instagram.

title: Contradiction and the Unknown Permeate Isaiah Lee's Imaginative Dollhouse Paintings
description: With a teal roof and gabled windows, a colonial-style dollhouse is at the center of Isaiah Lee’s practice. In his current body of work, the Chicag
body:
With a teal roof and gabled windows, a colonial-style dollhouse is at the center of Isaiah Lee’s practice. In his current body of work, the Chicago artist renders childhood toys that transition from objects of play and nostalgia into uncanny, animate entities. Set in the scaled-down rooms and landscape around the miniature home, Lee’s scenes channel the wonder and theatrics of the adolescent imagination, while confronting the ways these early experiences permeate one’s life.
Born into a fundamentalist Christian family in Missouri, the artist grapples with the contradictions within the teachings of his upbringing, alongside the lived reality of being a Black man in the U.S. In “Shepherd I,” a tiny green astronaut evokes Moses as he leads livestock through the house, while an enormous skull and concealed man loom in the shadows. The vast differences in scale within a single scene gesture toward the outsized impact of some encounters and how our memories have the capability of exaggerating the scope.
“Shepherd I”
Narrative ripples throughout Lee’s paintings, with “Romeo and Juliet” and “Juliet” capturing two different points of view of the same scene. The artist’s ability to shift perspectives is a compelling world-building technique and, like his heavy use of shadow, positions each composition as an illuminated nook amid a vast network of the unknown. “They arrive at a moment when it feels necessary to return to childhood as a way of uncovering who we are and what good we are still capable of bringing forth,” he adds. 
Darkness pervades many of the pieces, not necessarily in a sinister way but instead to suggest the omnipresence of the unknown and a sense of underlying fear. He writes that “faith cannot simply be abandoned but must be understood as an inheritance wrought into the body and the imagination.”
Lee is preparing for a solo exhibition this fall at crosswalk in Chicago. Titled A Thief in the Night, the show nods to the Biblical notion that people need to repent in order to be “right with the Lord.” “For many, this warning creates a persistent sense of unease, fostering the belief that no amount of faithfulness is truly enough,” the artist says. “Life becomes a race against time, a race that cannot be won.”
If you’re in Chicago, you can see some of Lee’s works through November 1 in an exhibition celebrating the city’s emerging artists at Hyde Park Art Center, and A Thief in the Night opens on October 16. Find more on Instagram.

title: Jennifer Higgie’s Empathetic Elegy for Richard Dadd
description:
Book Review
                 In “Bedlam,” the author and art critic does not describe the English painter’s often-sensationalize
body:
Book Review
                 In “Bedlam,” the author and art critic does not describe the English painter’s often-sensationalized mental deterioration. Instead, she writes the novel in his voice.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Richard Dadd, "Bacchanalian Scene" (1862) (image public domain US CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)In English painter Richard Dadd’s “The Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke” (1855–64), the ghostly, gray faces of well-dressed Victorians nestle among human-size dandelions and shrubs, partially obscuring a shrouded figure raising an axe overhead. The eerie work was painted at Broadmoor Hospital, a high-security psychiatric institution where Dadd was confined after his tenure at the famed Bethlem Royal Hospital, also known as “Bedlam.” Writer and art critic Jennifer Higgie captures a similarly uncanny world in her novel of the same name. Originally published by Sternberg Press in 2006 and re-released by Verso in July, Bedlam reimagines the painter’s infamous 1842 expedition through Europe, Southwest Asia, and North Africa as a draughtsman for a British nobleman, a journey that spurred a period of psychosis and resulted in Dadd committing patricide at age 26. It’s this dark odyssey that propels Higgie’s fragmented, first-person account. Through diaristic, idiosyncratic snapshots, she translates Dadd’s uncanny, often Orientalist paintings and drawings into “his” own writing. Higgie’s bold approach illuminates the fragile boundaries between historically marginalized minds like Dadd’s and those of people who may never see the inside of a psychiatrist’s office. Truth and fiction merge and disjoint as Dadd moves toward crisis, a visceral and strange descent emphasized by Higgie’s choice to embody — not mediate or describe — his perspective. As Dadd says in Bedlam’s opening salvo from Broadmoor Hospital, “Perhaps it is the story that chooses the man … I did not write my life.” But Higgie did. In her telling, Dadd’s psychosis emerges from the artist’s increasingly off-kilter understanding of the relationship between reality and its representations. Tasked with capturing his international trip in sketches for Sir Thomas Phillips, Dadd wonders why he should “bother” to recreate the Alps in front of him if his drawings “can’t help but be inferior to the original,” ultimately soothing himself with the idea that “a drawing is simply another mountain.” He agonizes over the differences between what he draws and what he sees: “In every wave a picture hides from me, but none I can mention or describe to my companion,” he says, traveling across the Gulf of Corinth. Later, near En Gedi, a desert near the Dead Sea and present-day Occupied West Bank, metaphors collapse into hallucination. “I see scorpions the size of men haunting ruins,” he says. “I crash into walls I do not see.”  Richard Dadd, "The Fairy Feller's Master-Stroke" (1855–64), oil on canvas (image public domain US CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

title: Catherine Murphy Has Her Cake and Eats It Too
description:
Feature
                The painter reconciles modernist conventions like the grid with one-point perspective, creating somethin
body:
Feature
                The painter reconciles modernist conventions like the grid with one-point perspective, creating something fresh and entirely her own. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Detail of Catherine Murphy, “One-eighty” (2026) (all photos © Catherine Murphy; photo Al Nowak; courtesy the artist, Peter Freeman, Inc., New York / Paris and Sadie Coles HQ, London)
    
        
            POUGHKEEPSIE, N.Y. — I first saw Catherine Murphy’s work at the now-defunct Xavier Fourcade gallery on Manhattan’s Upper East Side in 1980, and I have admired it ever since. Her career began when her paintings were included in the 1972 Annual Exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art (a precursor to the Biennial). Since then, Murphy has characterized herself as an “observational painter” who bases her work on what she sees. Throughout her career, however, she would move from what she saw to setting up situations based on dreams and memory, broadening the definition of realism as well as breaking with the realist painting convention of working on a one-to-one scale. With these two innovations, Murphy single-handedly pushed observational painting into a fertile territory that is all her own. Like Alex Katz, whose paintings she saw as a student, Murphy wanted to make large paintings that could hold their own next to the Abstract Expressionists and, in opposition to them, reject style and working in series.While I have written about Murphy many times, including in the only monograph on her paintings and drawings, I continue to find the richness and perceptual complexity of her works wonderfully daunting. Whether I am looking at two clear plastic bags filled with used clothes, stacked on a broken office chair; stacks of books with yellowed pages, seen from the side; or a wallpapered corner of a room with baseboard and red wall-to-wall carpet, I always feel like I am just scratching the surface. While I have long focused on her attention to detail within the overall view, it recently struck me that I had not paid enough attention to the structure of the paintings, and that the friction between the entire picture and its parts was another of the innovations for which Murphy deserves recognition.Catherine Murphy, "Jars" (2026), graphite on paperWhat I am proposing is that after breaking with the conventions governing realism, Murphy recognized that her ambition was even larger than her accomplishments. To keep moving, she had to take on the modernist conventions controlling abstraction, including the grid and the two-dimensional picture plane. Could they be reconciled with one-point perspective while being transformed into something fresh? Simply put: Murphy wanted to have her cake and eat it too. This meant she had to further articulate a trajectory that was hers alone, even as it brought pictorial challenges none of her contemporaries were addressing. To attain a rapprochement between realism and abstraction that had not been thought possible, she had to forgo the certainties she earned in her singular paintings and break new ground.Murphy is a subversive painter who has made work in dialogue with Renaissance painters and classical subjects, such as the nude, as well as work by her peers and generations before, including Lois Dodd and Robert Mangold. Refusing to embrace the postmodern ideology that all is rubble, or that the utopian ideal of progress is dead, Murphy rejected the by-now-familiar strategies of parody, citation, and irony. She was not interested in mocking high modernist motifs, but rather in utilizing modernist compositional devices, such as the grid, to revamp the mundane into the unexpected. In making realism (the three-dimensional) and modernism (the two-dimensional plane) inseparable, she could shape and honor time passing without seeking sanctuary from inevitable destruction; this became a lifelong preoccupation. It is what makes her paintings so engaging. Confronted by her scrupulously formal arrangement of telling particulars, at once isolated and connected, we see something of ourselves in her work — the inevitability of mortality and solitude.
